etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hopen, from Old English hopian (“hope”), from Proto-West Germanic *hopōn, further etymology unclear.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, transitive) To want something to happen, with a sense of expectation that it might.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter X, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: He looked round the poor room, at the distempered walls, and the bad engravings in meretricious frames, the crinkly paper and wax flowers on the chiffonier; and he thought of a room like Father Bryan's, with panelling, with cut glass, with tulips in silver pots, such a room as he had hoped to have for his own.

quote.citation: 1961 October, “The winter timetables of British Railways: Southern Region”, in Trains Illustrated, page 593:
quote.text: It is to be hoped that some corresponding smartening up of these other schedules may be expected before long.

quote.citation: 2013 June 8, “Obama goes troll-hunting”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8839, page 55:
quote.text: The solitary, lumbering trolls of Scandinavian mythology would sometimes be turned to stone by exposure to sunlight. Barack Obama is hoping that several measures announced on June 4th will have a similarly paralysing effect on their modern incarnation, the patent troll.

definitions.definition: To be optimistic; be full of hope; have hopes.
(intransitive) To place confidence; to trust with confident expectation of good; usually followed by in.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Psalms cxix:81:
1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Psalms xlii:11:
quote.text: Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? Hope thou in God.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hope, from Old English hopa (“hope, expectation”), from the same source as the verb hope.

definitions.definition: (countable or uncountable) The feeling of trust, confidence, belief or expectation that something wished for can or will happen.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter III, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: My hopes wa'n't disappointed. I never saw clams thicker than they was along them inshore flats. I filled my dreener in no time, and then it come to me that 'twouldn't be a bad idee to get a lot more, take 'em with me to Wellmouth, and peddle 'em out.

definitions.definition: (countable) A person or thing that is a source of hope.

We still have one hope left: my roommate might see the note I left on the table.

definitions.definition: (Christianity, uncountable) The virtuous desire for future good.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 1 Corinthians 13:13:
quote.text: But now abideth faith, hope, love, these three; and the greatest of these is love.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hope (“a valley”), from Old English hōp (found only in placenames). More at hoop.

definitions.definition: (Should we move, merge or split(+) this sense?) (Northern England, Scotland) A hollow; a valley, especially the upper end of a narrow mountain valley when it is nearly encircled by smooth, green slopes; a combe.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Icelandic hóp (“a small bay or inlet”). Cognate with English hoop.

definitions.definition: (Should we move, merge or split(+) this sense?) A sloping plain between mountain ridges.
(Scotland) A small bay; an inlet; a haven.

quote.text: Being by contrarie winds driuen to staie against Erith, at Grauesend, in Tilberie hope.

quote.citation: 1819, Jedediah Cleishbotham [pseudonym; Walter Scott], Tales of My Landlord, Third Series. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to IV), Edinburgh:  […]  [James Ballantyne and Co.] for Archibald Constable and Co.; London: Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, […]; Hurst, Robinson, and Co. […], →OCLC:
quote.text: A little hamlet which straggled along the side of a creek formed by the discharge of a small brook into the sea […] It was called Wolf's Hope (i.e. Wolf's Haven).
